title: A decade of manta ray research and conservation in Indonesia

authors.affiliation: Marine Megafauna Foundation, West Palm Beach, Florida, United States of America; Centre for Sustainable Aquatic Ecosystems, Harry Butler Institute, Murdoch University, Perth, Western Australia, Australia; Environmental and Conservation Sciences, Murdoch University, Perth, Western Australia, Australia
Marine Mammal Research Program, Hawaii Institute of Marine Biology, University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, Hawaii, United States

abstract_text:
Manta rays have some of the lowest estimated population growth rates for elasmobranchs, making them susceptible to drastic declines from human threats. A decade ago, Indonesia simultaneously hosted one of the largest fisheries for mantas, along with a major manta ray tourism industry. The high value of tourism was a strong argument for protection, but knowledge of habitat use was necessary to create effective policy. Galvanizing tourism operators and the public, we used citizen science to address knowledge gaps, identify manta ray hotspots, and provide baseline population data. We showed that manta rays routinely moved beyond established conservation and tourism areas into areas of high fishing activity, warranting nationwide species protection. That was then legislated in 2014.

Subsequently, we have provided longer-term characterizations of the habitat use, demographics, and remaining human threats to manta ray aggregations within the Nusa Penida Marine Protected Area (MPA) and the Komodo National Park (NP). Using a combination of active researcher and citizen science we established a high degree of site affinity to two sites within the Nusa Penida MPA. One site was crucial for adult cleaning and mating, and the other for feeding juveniles. Habitat use in Komodo NP follows a similar pattern, with four key sites identified.

Ongoing threats to manta rays in these areas include entanglement in fishing gear, plastic pollution, and growing tourism. Future research aims to assess population dynamics and trends, and to characterize additional critical habitats in the region.

title: Much ado about stingrays
abstract_text: This presentation intends to showcase the works completed during my MSc by research projects concerning the stingrays of southern Mozambique, the research gaps I have identified therein and the preliminary results of my forthcoming PhD projects. I intend to summarise the findings of the two published manuscripts from my MSc studies; the first detailing the validation of the computer-aided, photo-identification of the smalleye stingray, Megatrygon microps, which is among the largest and most unique species of stingrays in the world. The second manuscript describes the trends in the sightings of stingray in southern Mozambique, using citizen-science collected data to determine seasonality and small-scale habitat movement of stingrays in the diving region of Tofo, Mozambique. I am now undergoing PhD research to continue to work on filling the many research gaps that I have identified during the MSc work. My PhD topics include the use of stable isotope analysis to determine feeding ecology, habitat use and movements of multiple stingray species in the Inhambane provincial region. These data will compliment the photo-ID and diver observations already completed, whilst increasing our knowledge surrounding the differing trophic roles of each stingray species, their importance to the ecosystem and, most notably, reveal more about their movements to the ocean zones that are unavailable with the satellite and acoustic tags traditionally used in movement telemetry studies.

title: UK recreational shark angler practices, perceptions and attitudes; bridging the gap between scientists and anglers for the benefit of sharks
abstract_text: Recreational anglers are important stakeholders in global fisheries and have capacity to provide valuable data for scientific research and conservation management of threatened species. Recreational angling for sharks has a long history in the UK, and is seeing a renewed surge in popularity, but tensions exist between anglers and scientists over mistrust of how data will be used and issues around some cases of poor shark handling. The result has been a loss of data sharing and a stymied understanding of UK shark populations, especially for several threatened species that are considered data-poor. Here we present the results of the first project initiated by a new collaboration ‘Shark Hub UK’, which aims to bring anglers and scientists together as equals, for sharks. Our questionnaire was completed by 169 anglers from right around the UK and provided novel insights into the distribution and intensity of recreational angling activities for UK sharks, the handling methods currently employed and angler attitudes towards shark management and data sharing. The results will guide future shark handling best-practice guidance for anglers, rebuild trust between anglers and scientists, and highlight avenues for key future research into UK shark ecology and conservation.

title: Biodiversity and conservation of elasmobranchs in Watamu Marine National Park, Kenya
abstract_text:
The no-take MPA in Watamu Kenya houses a diversity of IUCN Red List threatened elasmobranchs and serves as a nursery area for at least one of these species. The surrounding community is growing in its understanding of the intrinsic and natural capital value of these species through creative educational opportunities both in schools and among artisanal fishers.

Ten elasmobranch species were observed using four methods (BRUVs, Timed Swims, Beach walks, and Diving surveys): Taeniura lymma, Glaucostegus halavi, Carcharhinus melanopterus, Neotrygon caeruleopunctata, Himantura gerrardi, Himantura uarnak, Triaenodon obesus, Torpedo sinuspersici, Aetobatus narinari, and Rhincodon typus. The most abundant species were Carcharhinus melanopterus, Taeniura lymma, and Neotrygon caeruleopunctata. Elasmobranchs were observed most often over sand habitat (56%) followed by seagrass (33%), and coral (11%).

Larger Blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus), majority females were seen August – November. Most small pups appeared along the shallow sandy areas along the length of WMNP’s beach from October onwards with a decline of larger sharks around this time. Footage of a shark that appears to show afterbirth with a larger male following was recorded in early November possibly indicating WMNP as an important pupping ground.

Environmental education created awareness among community members. Programs were conducted in 8 schools reaching 320 students and 10 community groups reaching 237 individuals. An artisanal fishing competition was held for the first time which involved the use of hooks of a specific size to emphasize the importance of sustainable fishing methods and conservation of elasmobranchs.

title: A cross-disciplinary approach to the protection of South Africa’s threatened sharks and rays

authors.affiliation: Research Associate of University of KwaZulu-Natal

abstract_text: South Africa is a global hotspot for chondrichthyan diversity while providing important habitats for many threatened species. Despite a rich history of shark research and management in South Africa, there are knowledge gaps, inadequate statutory interventions ensuring adequate protection, and a lack of capacity to effectively enforce current legal provisions. Furthermore, public perceptions about sharks are in general, negative, and based on incorrect information. To improve the protection of threatened (Vulnerable, Endangered, and Critically Endangered) species, prioritizing South African endemics, the WILDTRUST through their marine programme, WILDOCEANS, together with the Shark Conservation Fund and many other partners, implemented a 3-year Shark and Ray Protection Project. A campaign called Shark Attack was launched in March 2020, highlighting the plight of South Africa’s chondrichthyans and actively attempting to shift negative perceptions and inspire positive action through its website, social media platforms, and traditional media. The following content are available for download online: database and annotated checklist comprising all known chondrichthyan species found in South African waters, detailed status reports on 90 threatened and/or endemic species, a field guide of threatened and endemic species for law enforcement officers, online species ID workshops, draft recommendations for improved statutory modifications to SA legislation, shark and ray systematic conservation plan report, with associated R-scripts, highlighting essential habitats for shark and ray MPA’s or shark sanctuaries, trade toolkit for law enforcement in numerous ports of entry and various information pack and policy brief for decision-makers. The presentation aims to highlight the successes of this collaborative project.

title: Quantifying angler perceptions about shark depredation through stakeholder engagement
abstract_text: The Gulf of Mexico (GoM) is home to 31 federally managed reef fish species that are both commercially and recreationally important for communities in the region. These fish are federally managed through a series of stock assessments and a scientific understanding of natural lifecycles. Depredation, defined as the partial or complete removal of a captured species by a non-target species, is a cause of increased mortality and is not well quantified or understood. Mounting voices from anglers in the community suggest depredation is not only a prevalent and pervasive issue across the Gulf but also is rapidly increasing. Because of this, fisheries managers cannot effectively capture true population numbers derived from stock assessments. Depredation is a complex social-ecological issue that occurs between a multitude of species and is not required to be reported. Therefore, we have turned to anglers across the GoM to gain insights into their perceptions, interactions, and identification of the main causes and drivers of depredation to better assist in the classification and characterization to increase the accuracy of fisheries managers’ stock assessments. To do this, we distributed a Gulf-wide survey (n = 1044) that focused on building cognitive maps to highlight the perceptions anglers have on depredation. We also asked questions that quantified key factors that have influenced depredation, such as seasonal variation and fishing habits, to better understand the human-wildlife conflict that depredation is causing. Using the information gathered, we can begin to more accurately assess how depredation impacts anglers and stock assessments.

title: Trophic ecology and coastal habitat use of two sympatric shark species in the Azores archipelago (mid-Atlantic) assessed with CNS stable isotope analysis

authors.affiliation: GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel
CCMAR – Centre of Marine Sciences, University of Algarve

abstract_text: The anthropogenic exploitation of marine resources has caused drastic declines of large predatory fishes. Amongst these, sharks are of major conservation concern due to their high vulnerability to overfishing and role as top predators. The Azores Islands, Mid Atlantic, are thought to serve as essential fish habitat (EFH - waters necessary to fish for spawning, breeding, feeding or growth to maturity) for tope (Galeorhinus galeus) and smooth hammerhead (Sphyrna zygaena) sharks, but data to better assess this role are scarce. To address existing knowledge gaps, here we provide the first comparative assessment of the trophic ecology, ontogenetic shifts with increasing shark size and niche partitioning of G. galeus and S. zygeana around the Azores based on simultaneous δ13C, δ15N and δ34S (CNS) stable isotope analysis. Overall, shark isotopic niches, obtained using a 3D-Bayesian ellipse approach, indicated a strong role of mixed coastal-benthic resources, but with clear differences between life stages consistent with intra- and interspecific niche partitioning. Whereas tope shark showed a significant ontogenetic shift to higher trophic levels within the coastal-benthic prey niche, smooth hammerhead sharks exhibited significant decreases in δ34S, consistent with an increasing reliance on coastal-benthic prey with growing size. The co-occurrence of juveniles of two shark species of high conservation concern, and the role of coastal-benthic prey in their diet, highlight the importance of healthy coastal habitats for the conservation of these emblematic predators in the wider Atlantic, and of the important role of Azores coastal areas as EFH.

title: Morphology influences niche dynamics in two large sympatric sharks from Uruguayan waters

abstract_text: Prey availability in an environment does not ensure that prey will be consumed by a predator, as they must also be detected, captured and handled. Predator morphology imposes limitations on prey selection due to biomechanical constraints, making some prey functionally inaccessible and thereby shaping predators’ trophic niches. We assessed how two important components of morphology (tooth shape and body length) influence prey selectivity and trophic niche in two large-bodied sympatric sharks with contrasting feeding modes. The first species capture prey using spear-shaped, grasping teeth (Carcharias taurus), while the second has multi-cuspid cutting teeth used to serrate larger prey (Notorynchus cepedianus). Stomach content analysis and isotopic values of δ13C, δ34S and δ15N from muscle and liver were used to characterize trophic niche and prey selection. As gape-limited C. taurus grew, their consumption of teleosts decreased inversely to chondrichthyans. By contrast, non-gape limited N. cepedianus consumed teleosts and chondrichthyans in similar proportions, along with marine mammals, but with no clear relationship to body size. As body length increased, both species consumed prey from higher trophic levels (higher δ15N), but N. cepedianus accessed prey at relatively higher trophic levels. δ13C and δ34S remained substantially unchanged with body length since gape and dentition are less limiting for these tracers. Morphological characters play an essential role in predator prey selection and may be the primary mechanism facilitating resource partitioning in marine predators. Their inclusion in ecological studies will help understand prey choice and how it shapes trophodynamics in marine ecosystems.

title: Using biologgers to estimate energy expenditure and consumption rates of great hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna mokarran)
abstract_text: Top predators play an important role in ecosystem food webs, and quantifying predators’ energetic needs is key to understanding their rate of consumption on lower tropic levels. Metabolic costs are the largest components of an organism’s energy budget, and measuring an organism’s metabolic rate in the field provides an estimate of how much an organism must consume. We used biologgers to record depth, temperature, speed, tri-axial acceleration and tri-axial magnetism of great hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna mokarran) tagged off of the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of Florida. We then used previously-established hydrodynamic models of great hammerheads derived from wind tunnel experiments to convert measures of swim speed from sampled sharks into energy consumption rates. Preliminary analysis of four sharks indicate sampled individuals would need to consume an average of approximately 1.27 lbs of food per day to account for metabolic costs, varying with speed and size of the animal. These results further our understanding of the ecological role of great hammerheads, a critically endangered predator, by allowing us to calculate how much prey they may be removing from local ecosystems.

title: Breaking bags and crunching clams: Assessing whitespotted eagle ray interactions with shellfish aquaculture gear

authors.affiliation: Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, Florida Atlantic University
Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science, University of Miami
Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, Florida Atlantic University
Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, Florida Atlantic University

abstract_text: Shallow coastal waters are commonly used in shellfish aquaculture for “grow-out” of bivalves like the Northern Quahog (Mercenaria mercenaria). These grow-out locations have substantially higher clam densities than the surrounding environment and potentially attract molluscivores. Inspired by clammer reports of predator-inflicted damage to grow-out gear, we assessed the capacity of a highly mobile predator (whitespotted eagle ray Aetobatus narinari) to detect and interact with clams housed within a suite of industry standard antipredator materials. Experiments were conducted in mesocosms where rays were exposed to unprotected clams (control), clams inside polyester mesh clam bags (dipped in a latex net coating and non-dipped), and under high density polyethylene (HDPE) or chicken wire cover netting. Gear interactions were quantified from video footage throughout the course of the experiment and clam mortality was assessed after its completion. Rays interacted with antipredator gear significantly more than control plots, with particularly long durations noted for clam bags covered with HDPE netting. While rays were capable of consuming clams through bags, antipredator treatments reduced clam mortality by 4-10x compared to control plots. Double-layered (i.e., bags with cover netting) treatments exhibited the lowest clam mortality (0.6±0.1%), highlighting the utility of this type of protection in shellfish aquaculture.

title: A comparison of deep-sea sharks trophic ecology over large spatial scales
abstract_text:
An important diversity of sharks lives in the depths of the oceans around the world. The trophic ecology of these species is still poorly known due to the difficulties to access this remote environment and observing individuals directly. Indirect observations have proven useful in addressing this issues through the use of stomach contents analyses mainly. This method provides essential information but is subjected to a series of biases: only recent prey can be observed, different tissues have different digestion rates and a lot of stomachs might be empty. Other approaches such as stable isotopes (SIA) or fatty acid profiling (FAP) are more and more recognized to achieve more comprehensive ecological data.

We used SIA to explore the trophic ecology of different deep-sea shark communities across the world. A total of 21 species were considered, coming from five locations separated by large distances: Chatham Rise plateau in New Zealand, Taiwan, Kerguelen Islands, Gascogne strait and Mediterranean Sea. δ13C, δ15N, and δ34S isotope ratios were measured on muscle and liver samples after lipid, TMAO and urea extraction. Isotopic niches were then calculated using Bayesian statistical methods. The ecological inferences were compared between the different locations, considering parameters such as spatial scale, latitude, longitude or taxonomic classification to try and explain the similitude and differences observed. This work was supported by a travel research grant from FNRS Belgium.

title: Shark Lab Education and Outreach
abstract_text: The Shark Lab has long been a keystone in elasmobranch research in the local Long Beach community and global shark knowledge. With so much innovation in new technology and research techniques to study behavior and ecology of marine animals, the lab has a wealth of scientific findings to make readily available and applicable to the public and students of all ages. Our mobile outreach program, called Shark Shacks, travels across southern California beaches and ocean piers to reach thousands of beachgoers and lifeguards. Additionally, the Shark Lab has begun to implement new educational programs specific to K-12 classrooms focusing on getting students interested in Science, Technology, Engineering and Math (STEM). Beginning with virtual and transitioning to in-person programming, curricula encompass content covering shark biology, technology, and careers in these STEM fields. Our outreach and education efforts are focused on informing beach goers across all ages about shark behavior and how to stay safe while enjoying the ocean. For K-12 students, the goal of the lab is to increase access to dynamic and interesting fields across disciplines and invoke excitement about fields they may have never seen themselves in. All our programming is free of charge and open to diverse audiences across southern California and beyond.

title: The Global Shark Census - can citizen science add value to research?
abstract_text:
One of the fastest growing fields in marine conservation is the development and expansion of citizen science projects. Shark and ray conservation is a particularly appealing field for citizen science projects, yet the majority of the existing programmes are uncoordinated and vary greatly in effort and level of participant expertise. The recent review of emergent research and priorities for shark and ray conservation (Jorgensen et al. 2022) identified an urgent need to increase coordination, leadership and collaboration between scientists, governments and community groups.

PADI (The Professional Association of Diving Instructors) and The PADI AWARE Foundation have a successful track record of developing and implementing successful large-scale citizen science initiatives. Our existing Dive Against Debris has been successful in coordinating the global efforts of millions of divers conducting marine debris surveys, leading to data contributing towards ground-breaking research.

In 2023, the PADI AWARE Foundation will seek to replicate the success of Dive Against Debris and launch the Global Shark Census. This initiative aims to coordinate the efforts of PADI’s global network of 6,600 dive centres, 128,000 PADI Professionals and 15 million registered and active PADI divers to collect shark and ray datasets that will actively contribute towards the development of management measures, augment academic research and bring scale to conservation advocacy. This presentation will outline the opportunities to harness data collection on an unprecedented scale.

title: Mining social media for Elasmobranch fishery data in conflict zones: The Gaza strip as a case study
abstract_text: A huge gap in environmental information exists in conflict regions where environmental access to scientists ranges from unsafe to impossible. Previously unknown knowledge of Elasmobranchii presence, composition, and distribution can provide valuable information regarding the exploitation of elasmobranch species and for creating comprehensive conservation strategies. However, the diversity, ecology, behavior, and many other characteristics of these species in conflict zones remain virtually unknown, which is a major cause for concern. Traditional species surveys rely on in-situ observations and municipality regulations forcing fisheries to self-report their catch. Conflict areas present a unique challenge, lacking formal regulation or scientific access. Here, we report the first use of social media monitoring (“iEcology”) of the extent of the Elasmobranch fishery in the Gaza strip, a conflict region previously lacking any information. Our database consists of 3 years of daily reported catch from 8 markets in the Gaza strip. We collected 584 data points belonging to 2348 individuals of 14 species. The analysis of the data suggests temporal, spatial, and seasonal trends in elasmobranch catch distribution are affected by changes in the access to maritime areas due to local conflict escalations and de-escalations. We demonstrate this approach as a relatively accurate and inexpensive data analysis procedure, allowing the quantification and normalization of multiple unrelated observations of caught and targeted fish into a uniformed geo-spatial-temporal system - making it a prime candidate for future endeavors in other conflict zones in coastal regions.

title: Research, educate, and explore the world with sharks and field school
abstract_text: Studies have shown that STEM education leads to better public perceptions and understanding of science and the broader impact of its role in society. As charismatic species, sharks and rays can be used as ambassador species for increasing the reach of both STEM and ocean education. This talk will present the programs, experiences, and lessons to date from Field School and the Field School Foundation, a set of hybrid research-education programs operating in Miami-Dade, Florida and centered on that community’s connections to Biscayne Bay. Biscayne Bay is a large, fragile marine estuary with considerable marine biodiversity, including of several endangered elasmobranch species. To communicate the role that sharks have in the ocean and educate families on the impact they are having on them, accessible resources are needed. Through a combination of student and citizen science participation and ready-to-deploy classroom lesson plans that integrate the research program and local ecosystems, these programs help to teach data and ocean literacy, build communication skills, and develop locally-relevant STEM curriculum that differentiates research for general audiences at multiple levels. Field School creates a safe and inclusive environment for students to learn and develop hands-on skills, as students apply what they are learning and seeing the impact they have first hand. Our education programs and curriculum are free, and available for students of all ages, to connect people locally and globally to sharks in Biscayne Bay, Florida, as we research, educate, and explore, the world of sharks together.

title: Global phylogeography and population genomics of the commercially exploited smoothhound shark

authors.affiliation: The Norwegian Institute of Bioeconomy Research

abstract_text: Accelerated global warming and over-exploitation of marine species threaten to eradicate the unique genetic archives of modern Chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimeras), an evolutionarily robust lineage with a 400-million-year genealogy. Understanding the impact of rapidly changing global conditions on elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) and devising conservation responses relies on the identification of unique genetic populations adapted to specific environmental niches. This research focuses on delineating the global phylogeography of the common smoothhound shark, Mustelus mustelus, using whole mitogenome data from 9 sampling populations collected across the species’ distribution range. The same samples have been used to generate reduced-representation sequencing (RRS) (RADSeq) data in order to reveal associations between single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) alleles and environmental variables hypothesized to drive selection while controlling for the confounding effects of neutral genetic structure. It is predicted that species inhabiting the rapidly warming, yet diverse, biogeographic regions of South Africa and the Mediterranean Sea are likely locally adapted to their environment which can lead to differences in genetic variation among populations even in the face of high gene flow. The eventual goal is to better characterize the genomic mechanisms of environmental adaptation and provide a system for predicting responses to new selective challenges in this species and exploited houndsharks. The mitogenomes of four such species have been sequenced and submitted for publication, providing an opportunity to increase the resolution of phylogenomic studies and conduct more extensive population genomics investigations to better inform management strategies.

title: Genomic investigation and kinship provide insights into a highly mobile shark
abstract_text:
Spurdog (Squalus acanthias) are a wide-ranging, highly mobile, small shark found in temperate seas across the globe. Once a commercially important species, they have experienced severe declines and are now listed as Endangered in the Northeast Atlantic. Despite a zero total allowable catch, they can be caught as bycatch, which as an aggregating species, can comprise of up to <10 tonnes in a single catch. This may impact population size, with subsequent effects on genetic diversity.

Previous research using microsatellite markers suggested that aggregations may contain closely related individuals. As the loss of kin groups can rapidly erode selectable genetic diversity, understanding the genetic composition of spurdog across the British Isles is crucial to assess the potential impact of their removal by fishing on population sustainability. Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) markers are being used to understand the genetic diversity and population structuring of spurdog across the British Isles. Kinship will also be investigated to reveal whether relations are found within sampled aggregations. This may subsequently provide insight into their aggregating behaviour, in terms of origin and persistence as a group, as well as the genetic diversity of the spurdog that they represent.

title: Global population genomics assessment of the critically endangered great hammerhead shark

authors.affiliation: Save Our Seas Foundation Shark Research Center, Nova Southeastern University
Save Our Seas Foundation Shark Research Center, Nova Southeastern University
Save Our Seas Foundation Shark Research Center, Nova Southeastern University

abstract_text: The great hammerhead (Sphyrna mokarran) is an iconic, large-bodied shark species distributed worldwide in tropical to warm temperate seas, in habitats ranging from coastal to semi-oceanic waters. Great hammerhead shark fins have high value in the international fin trade. Overexploitation coupled with high bycatch mortality has caused steep declines in much of its distribution, resulting in an IUCN Red List assessment of great hammerheads as “Critically Endangered” globally. Since little knowledge existed about the population genetic dynamics of this species to inform conservation management, we used a high-resolution, bi-organelle, genomics approach to assess the population structure and genetic diversity of this species across large parts of its global distribution. Analyses with Single Nucleotide Polymorphism markers (n=162; 1816 SNPs) revealed three highly distinct global populations, comprising great hammerheads from the Western Atlantic, Red Sea/Persian Gulf and east/west Australian coasts, with no population structure observed within these large regions. Analyses using 176 complete mitochondrial genome sequences (mitogenomes), in contrast, revealed matrilineal genetic distinctiveness on smaller spatial scales, including between the western North Atlantic and Caribbean, and within the western Indian Ocean, consistent with female philopatry. There was no evidence for population differentiation with either SNP or mitogenome markers between western and northeastern Australia sampled great hammerheads. Notably, global mitogenome-based phylogeographic analyses revealed that Australian great hammerheads are highly evolutionarily divergent from western Indian and western Atlantic conspecifics.

title: Screening the immune gene diversity of Cartilaginous fish – relevance to management and evolution
abstract_text: This talk showcases the relevance of studying immune genes in Cartilaginous fish, providing specific examples of their relevance to fisheries management and conservation, and to understand the evolution of this ancient group. Genetic diversity at immune genes is driven by pathogen-induced selection, leading to locally adapted populations and reduced migrant fitness. Thus, immune genes may be better at detecting biologically relevant population units compared to neutral markers (e.g. nuclear microsatellites), improving stock delimitation. Also, preserving immune gene diversity across populations is key to ensure their adaptive potential against future pathogens and environmental changes. These features make immune genes prime candidate markers in improving stock identification and the sustainable long-term management of vulnerable marine species. On the other hand, Chondrichthyans are the oldest living jawed vertebrates with the basic features of adaptive immunity; thus, they are a key group in the evolution of vertebrate adaptive immunity and are essential to identify its ancestral and derived features. Also, given the group´s long evolutionary history and remarkable ecological diversity, different lineages experienced different environmental stressors and pathogenic agents, perhaps resulting in different immune response mechanisms and genetic makeup. Here, we show results contrasting genetic diversity patterns at neutral vs. immune genes for commercially exploited shark species, and their implication to population structure reconstruction. We also uncover the high diversity of immune gene (MHC) lineages in Chondrichthyans compared to previous assumptions, and unravel how Chondrichthyan genomics contribute to reconstructing the primordial immune complex at the dawn of jawed vertebrates.

abstract_text: The survival of chondrichthyans is a major marine conservation concern, with over one-third of species currently at risk of extinction due to their exceptional vulnerability and low resilience to high levels of exploitation. However, our extremely limited knowledge of their basic ecology hampers the implementation of proper management and conservation actions. There is also a knowledge gap on the genetic diversity and population structure of these species at different spatial scales. This is especially true for migratory species that, at different stages of their life, depend on the restricted coastal habitats of oceanic islands. Understanding the degree of genetic connectivity allows to define population boundaries and infer dispersal patterns, while describing genetic diversity will allow to inform appropriate measures to preserve it. To fill this knowledge gap, we used a genetic multi-marker approach focused on two key migratory and endangered species of contrasting life histories and behavior: tope shark (Galeorhinus galeus) and sicklefin devil ray (Mobula tarapacana). We evaluated population structure and assessed connectivity at different spatial scales – from ocean basins to the island groups within the Azorean archipelago - through the analysis of Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) markers and Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). The results of this project will provide science-based knowledge to support suitable management and conservation actions, regionally and globally.

abstract_text: Hammerheads (Carcharhiniformes, Sphyrnidae) are a recent radiation of 10 described shark species, characterized by their laterally expanded head (“cephalofoil”). All hammerhead species are listed in threatened categories by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) due to overexploitation. Genetic analyses of one species, the bonnethead shark (S. tiburo) reveal that it is possibly a species complex, with one species occurring in the Western Atlantic from the U.S.A to Mexico and another occurring from Belize to Brazil. Morphometric, meristic, and genetic variation was used to examine differences between these cryptic species and describe them. Sixty-one morphometric measurements and three meristic characters (vertebral count, lower and upper rows of functional teeth) were taken from 23 bonnetheads, 12 from Placencia, Belize and 11 from Florida, U.S. For the morphometric data an allometric formula was used to standardize any effect caused by differences in size of the individuals. These data were analyzed with univariate and multivariate statistics. There were no significant differences in the morphology of the two species, however, there were non-overlapping vertebral counts between Florida and Belize specimens. Variation at two mitochondrial markers (cytochrome oxidase I and control region) and 12 nuclear microsatellite loci are also partitioned between these two species. The genetic and meristic characters clearly differentiate these species and enable formal descriptions of Sphyrna tiburo from the U.S.A. to Mexico, and S. alleni from Belize to Brazil. The latter is already likely threatened with extinction throughout its range.

title: Citizen science as a tool to get baseline ecological and biological data on sharks and rays in a data-poor region

abstract_text: The Mexican Caribbean is in one of the regions with the greatest diversity of elasmobranchs in the world. However, the population status of most of the shark and ray species in this region is unknown. We used a citizen science program based on divers to collect data about the diversity, abundance, and distribution of elasmobranchs in this region. We visited dive centers in six locations and performed structured interviews with divemasters, instructors, and owners of the diving centers. In total, 79 divers were interviewed, of which 69% had more than five years’ experience diving in the Mexican Caribbean. Divers could identify 24 elasmobranch species for this region. Most of the divers (82%) reported a decrease in sightings of sharks and rays. Rays were the most frequently sighted species by divers (89%), and the spotted eagle ray (A. narinari) was the most common elasmobranch species reported in the region. Citizen science was a useful approach gathering for baseline information about sharks and rays in the Mexican Caribbean, increasing our knowledge of the abundance and distribution of some species in this region. Citizen science affords the opportunity to obtain long-term data that can be useful for management and conservation.

abstract_text: Socioecological data on sharks is scant for many islands of Latin America. Our goal is to develop baseline information on the diversity and presence of sharks through time. On Cozumel, The Arrecifes de Cozumel National Park and the Isla de Cozumel Flora and Fauna Protection Area have high biodiversity and interconnectivity between ecosystems as mangroves, seagrasses, and coral reefs part of the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef. Since 2021 we have collected 90 Local Ecological Knowledge (LEK) fishers' surveys with a geospatial component. Scuba diving has been a central activity on the island since the 70s. Together with fishers' LEK, we are documenting divers' perceptions of the environment. In collaboration with diving enterprises, we have integrated a database with 45 records documenting shark sightings. Combining the above data using geospatial tools, we have over 15 polygons around the island where Nurse Shark (Ginglymostoma cirratum), Great Hammerhead Shark (Sphyrna mokarran), Scalloped Hammerhead Shark (Sphyrna lewini), Black Tip Shark (Carcharhinus limbatus), Caribbean Reef Shark (Carcharhinus perezi), and Tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier) have been documented. Preliminary underwater observations allowed establishing shark presence and qualitative descriptions of the aquatic habitats. Sharks' literature and historical pictures are being collected. Narratives manifested a decrease in shark presence during the last 15 years. Responses attribute this to excess maritime traffic and mass tourism. Our novel interdisciplinary data proves LEK can provide information on species' existence, behavior, and ecology. Preserving Cozumel's natural capital, including sharks, is critical given that local people depend on healthy ecosystems for their local economy and well-being.

abstract_text: Oceanic whitetip sharks (Carcharhinus longimanus) were listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act in 2018, and stock assessments indicate that populations in the western and central Pacific are historically and currently overfished. However, large data gaps remain in relation to the basic biology, ecology and population structure of this species. Photographic identification is a common and non-invasive method used to evaluate metrics of elasmobranch population demographics, abundance, residency and movement, and social behaviors. The main Hawaiian Islands are a known ‘hotspot’ for C. longimanus where they typically exhibit seasonal residency; a finding that is also supported by local fisher knowledge. This study describes the results of the Hawaii Community Tagging Program, a citizen science initiative in which fishers, divers and snorkelers submitted images of C. longimanus interactions around the main Hawaiian Islands beginning in 2008. Over 2000 images of C. longimanus were analyzed, and dorsal fin patterns were used to determine the number of unique and resighted individuals. To date, this study has identified 313 unique individuals with 15 resights; the sex ratio of females to males is approximately 2:1 (169 females and 81 males identified). We identified 45 females (~26%) with scarring or injuries from potential mating interactions and 85 individuals (~34%) carried evidence of previous fishing interactions. The information obtained from this study can help provide baseline information regarding the population demographics, residency and fishery interactions of C. longimanus around the main Hawaiian islands to help inform conservation and management measures for this protected species.

title: Whale shark tourism and conservation through citizen science
abstract_text: Whale sharks are globally threatened; in Peru, there is no further regulation for the species than a fishing ban. Since 2014, we have been working in northern Peru with local communities to create awareness and gather data of whale shark encounters. In 2018, we start training stakeholders, such as fishermen and tour operators in how to offer responsible whale shark tourism activities to help them improve their practice and to help us collect data for the project. We implemented workshops to present the Best Practice Guidelines, and to receive feedback. We used an ethogram to collect whale shark behavior related to the boat and swimmers during fieldwork, additionally in every encounter we recorded injuries if found. To date, we have trained 53 boat Capitan and crew, in data collection and we have recommended the best practices for observation and swimming with the species. During fieldwork, we found that 85% of the sharks react to the swimmers by changing direction (89%), diving (61%), and/or swimming faster (59%). Moreover, 88% of sharks were encountered with injuries or signs of being injured recently. The recommendations from the training workshops were collected, and together with our results, a manual for good practices for whale shark tourism was prepared for the Peruvian government which is now in its final stage of review.

title: Engaging Aquarium Scientists in Global Shark Conservation through the IUCN Shark Specialist Group’s Aquarium Working Group
abstract_text: Elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) face a range of conservation challenges contributing to extensive population declines. Consequently, there has been considerable global effort to address these declines and the IUCN’s Shark Specialist Group (SSG) has been central to many of these efforts by bringing together experts from around the world. For the first time, an Aquarium Working Group (AWG) has been formed within the SSG to recognize the role which public aquaria play in the conservation of sharks and rays. The AWG has nine members from around the world, and has identified four priority tasks: 1. Develop a position statement for the SSG on the role of aquariums in elasmobranch conservation. 2. Compile life history information from Critically Endangered elasmobranchs in aquariums to inform conservation action, with a focus on sawfishes, rhino rays (wedgefishes and guitarfishes), and south American freshwater stingrays. 3. Develop a SSG position statement on ex-situ elasmobranch release, rescue, and re-introduction. 4. Develop SSG messaging and graphics on elasmobranch conservation for aquarium exhibits, outreach, and education programs. In addition to introducing the AWG, we will present the findings of a global survey focused on the current extent of elasmobranch release, rescue, and re-introduction within the aquarium community.

title: Post-release survival of accidentally captured silky shark in tuna purse seiners
abstract_text: Tagging programs are key to evaluate post-release mortality of Endangered, Threatened, and Protected species that are caught incidentally in fishing operations. This work presents results of a tagging program conducted on purse seiners under ECHEBASTAR company, aimed at assessing post-release survival of silky sharks caught in association with tuna schools and released according to the Code of Good Practices. During two fishing trips sixty silky sharks were tagged (28 and 32 silky sharks in the first and second trip, respectively) with 37 SPATs and 23 MiniPATs, and blood samples were collected in 124 sharks for lactate concentration measurement to be used as an indicator of shark survival. A vitality index based on state and behavior at release was also assigned to all the sharks caught accidentally. The overall predicted survival of silky shark was close to 40% based on vitality index derived from tagged sharks. The overall survival rate predicted using lactate concentration threshold was more variable among trips going from 35% to 60% in the first and second trip, respectively. Shark survivorship decreased as the fishing operation advanced and vitality index declined. This post-release survival estimates duplicate previous estimations on purse seiners. The experience gained over time in the application of best practices and fauna release devices (i.e. the bycatch conveyor belt) installed on-board contributed to reducing shark mortality in the purse seiner fishery.

title: Reducing hammerhead bycatch in the Great Barrier Reef: testing alternatives to mesh nets
abstract_text: Mesh net fisheries can result in bycatch of species of conservation interest (SOCI) such as dugongs and hammerhead sharks. In the Great Barrier Reef, bycatch mortality of both SOCI and of undersized/unwanted fishes has severely affected the fishery's social license and has exacerbated conflict, especially with recreational fishers. However, trap type gears can help reduce mortality. Tunnel nets are large mobile fish traps that guide the catch into a tunnel where the catch remains free-swimming until brailling and sorting. Bycatch is released in very good condition. Larger species including SOCI such as marine turtles, sharks, and rays are prevented from entering the tunnel by large mesh grids, and remain free swimming in a holding area until release. Increasing regulatory pressure and public scrutiny of net fisheries in the Great Barrier Reef are driving efforts to find solutions to improve sustainability and community support for fisheries while maintaining fisher livelihoods. Here we describe the results of a small-scale feasibility trial using tunnel net gears in the shallow coastal waters of the Great Barrier Reef. Expert tunnel net fishers worked with local net fishers to trial and test the use of tunnel nets. The gear works, fishers can catch fish and SOCI species such as hammerheads and batoids were released unharmed. However, the suitability and feasibility of these gears requires careful consideration and while the gear is technically feasible, its commercial viability remains unknown. The perspectives and attitudes of commercial fishers and other stakeholders engaged during the trials will also be presented.

title: Ecology and fisheries vulnerability of the Munk’s devil ray in the Mexican Pacific

abstract_text: Munk’s pygmy devil ray (Mobula munkiana) are medium size, zooplanktivorous filter feeding elasmobranchs. Native to the Eastern Tropical Pacific and listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, their aggregative behavior exacerbates its captured as targeted catch and as incidental bycatch in both artisanal and large-scale fisheries. By employing multiple approaches (acoustic telemetry, stable isotopes, traditional tagging, and photometry), we collected data to complete life history gaps such as the identification of critical habitats, migratory routes, and aggregative behavior patterns at the Mexican Pacific. At the same time, we assess their rates of post-release mortality from artisanal gillnet fisheries in Mexico using acoustic tags to understand the population-level effects of survival due to fisheries impacts on this species. To date, results of acoustic tags in M. munkiana individuals (n=108), traditional tags (n=95), blood samples for isotopes analysis (n=69) and photometry surveys (n=60) have allow us to describe a nursery area within the Marine Protected Area of Espiritu Santo Archipelago, and a reproductive ground for the species in La Ventana Bay in Baja California Sur. Pupping and mating periods are linked to spring and summer (April to June) seasons. Size and sex segregation is present in this species, including a differentiation in their diet as they grow, switching from euphausiids to mysids as main prey. Migratory patterns repeat across four years connecting at least 2 different Marine Protected Areas in the southern Gulf of California.

abstract_text: The sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus) has a global distribution and is caught by commercial and recreational fishers. We assessed the post-release survival of sandbar sharks caught in longline surveys conducted in Western Australia (WA) using an integrated approach that combined the use of hook-timers, release condition staging, satellite tagging, and blood physiology (adrenocorticotropic hormone, corticosterone, and lactate). Of the 57 individuals examined, 88% were “alive and strong” with 100% initial survival when released after a maximum of four hours on the hook. Of the 13 satellite-tagged individuals, 100% survived. Sharks dived up to 307 m deep and showed cyclical depth movement patterns with some individuals moving up and down the water column both day and night, while others moved almost exclusively at night, corresponding with the movement patterns of squid, a common prey item of sandbar sharks. The concentration of blood metabolites did not show a linear pattern with time on hook. The 100% survival rate within four hours on the hooks suggests the use of longlines for surveying sandbar shark abundance has no deleterious consequences.

abstract_text: Fisheries bycatch is a significant threat to shark populations worldwide. Thus, understanding bycatch fates – if an animal is retained or discarded, dear or alive – is key information for estimating the bycatch impact on shark populations. Here, we analyze the data on fates of sharks caught in the Convention Area of three tuna Regional Fisheries Management Organizations (RFMO): Western Pacific (WCPFC), Indian (IOTC) and Atlantic (ICCAT) Oceans, to infer bycatch fate patterns between 2012 and 2018. We calculate fate proportions from each RFMO for 68 taxa identified at the genus or species level. We find substantial variation in the reported categories and post-capture fates across RFMOs. No sharks were reported retained in WCPFC, with sharks being either discarded alive (average 66%) or dead (average 33%). While live discards were the most frequent in IOTC, they report 15% retention on average. Live discards show an increasing trend in ICCAT over the same period, peaking at 25% in 2017. Given the different rates of observer coverage for each RFMO, we refrain from comparing bycatch fates across them. Regarding CITES-listed species, we observed 100% live discards of whale sharks in ICCAT and IOTC, while almost 100% retention of mako sharks caught by ICCAT managed vessels. Mako sharks were also the most frequently retained species in IOTC. Overall, our analysis demonstrates that ICCAT represents most shark retention across RFMOs, which primarily comprises mako sharks. We further note that our results are likely influenced by the scarcity of available observer data, especially in IOTC and ICCAT.

abstract_text: The bronze whaler or copper shark (Carcharhinus brachyurus) is a large coastal shark with a wide distribution across a highly heterogeneous environment and is one of the most exploited elasmobranchs in South Africa. Here the aim was to assess the distribution of neutral and adaptive genomic diversity in this vulnerable species in the South-East Atlantic and South-West Indian Ocean region using putatively neutral and candidate single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Samples were collected across a representative distribution range from the east coast of South Africa to Angola and prepared for massively parallel sequencing on an Illumina platform using a restriction site-associated DNA (3RAD) library preparation protocol. Generated sequencing reads were processed with an optimized bioinformatic pipeline and resulted in thousands of SNPs genotyped in 64 samples. The analyses of putatively neutral SNPs revealed moderate and evenly distributed levels of genomic diversity across sampling sites. Multivariate and clustering analyses demonstrated a high degree of gene flow with no significant population structuring among or within ocean basins. Genotype-environment analysis performed using redundancy analysis identified SNPs significantly associated with mean sea surface temperature, pH and oxygen. These candidate SNPs indicated the presence of at least two clusters and deep divergence between individuals from South Africa, Namibia and Angola. These results provide evidence for local adaptation to specific environmental conditions in a highly mobile shark despite high levels of gene flow. This is expected to inform management strategies and policy at the national and regional level for conservation of C. brachyurus populations.

title: Identification of shark species off the nigerian coast using dna barcoding

authors.affiliation: National Coffee Research Institute, Mukono Uganda

abstract_text: Nigeria is one of the shark fishing nations in Africa, but its catch data on elasmobranchs are still recorded in aggregates ‘sharks’ and ‘rays’ with no further species-specific details. The major reason for this is most of the shark specimens look identical in morphology and field identification of some closely related species is difficult. Also, fisheries managers and scientists find it tricky to identify poorly preserved and deteriorating specimens or those lacking the key diagnostic features for identification. This study used DNA barcoding as a method to identify shark species from four different landing areas off the Nigerian Coast and two major fish markets in Lagos, Nigeria. 128 dorsal fins were sampled. 27 of these did not provide successful sequence results, while 101 (77.7%) provided a Chondrichthyan sequence that was matched to reference specimens in a DNA barcode database. Three species of sharks were identified, with all three of CITES importance, (17.8% Critically Endangered, 61.4% Endangered, 20.8% Vulnerable). Fisheries managers can use this information to assist in identification and make informed decisions on conservation and management issues.

title: Development of a 12S marker gene database for the environmental DNA metabarcoding of marine megafauna
abstract_text:
All living organisms leave traces of DNA in their environments. This DNA can be released through urine, gametes, blood, mucus, skin loss etc. This DNA can be collected in the water column through filtration, and is then called environmental DNA or eDNA. The metabarcoding of this eDNA is a new technicque which can then be used to accurately estimate marine biodiversity with more accurate value, including rare, cryptic, elusive or invasive species.

The aim of this project is to obtain genetic sequences from sharks, skates, rays and marine mammals at a global scale with a view to assign species to their 12S mitochondrion barcodes from eDNA samples. The barcode database is the cornerstone of any eDNA study in conservation. Thus, we’re looking for collaborations with aquariums and museums worldwide to collect tissues (fin clip (1.5 x 0.5 cm) on the caudal fin or blood (200μL) store in pure alcohol or frozen for missing species. With this sample (at least two individuals from each species) we will be able to extract the DNA and then complete the 12S marker gene database for these species. The advantage with this technique in addition to revealing the dark diversity is to be non-invasive for the species. Ultimately it will improve the knowledge (biogeography, presence in marine reserves, depth) such a collaboration would make it possible to take advantage of the competences of each one for a common objective: the conservation of threatened species.

abstract_text: Due to their exceptional levels of functional genetic diversity, genes of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) represent ideal candidates to reveal genetic differentiation among geographical regions and ultimately improving genetic stock identification of commercially exploited shark species. In addition, from an evolutionary perspective, because of the major role of MHC in pathogen resistance, MHC diversity can be expected to be locally adapted to pathogens, resulting in a more pronounced genetic structure in these genes compared to neutral expectations. Alternatively, balancing selection at the geographic scale can lead to a weaker genetic structure compared to the neutral population structure if, for instance, prevailing pathogens are the same over the whole study area. To distinguish between these scenarios, we sequenced MHC-IIβ genes using high-throughput sequencing technology in an extensive number of small-spotted catsharks (Scyliorhinus canicula) sampled across the entire European geographic distribution (N=600). All samples were also genotyped with 11 neutral microsatellite markers as a baseline to contrast with MHC diversity and genetic structure. Our preliminary results suggest that this species has three different MHC-IIβ genes, with the typical characteristics of functional MHC-IIβ genes: high number of alleles and high sequence divergence between alleles. We also show that MHC diversity in catsharks vary across regions, probably involving both demographic and selective forces. This study provides interesting perspectives for the understanding of evolutionary mechanisms involved in MHC diversity but also shows that the MHC system provides prime markers to stock delimitation, which is essential knowledge for sustainable long-term management of vulnerable marine species.

title: The xenobiotic biomonitor potential of the small spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula): a year long evaluation on heavy metal and microplastic accumulation
abstract_text: The small-spotted catshark Scyliorhinus canicula, is a demersal Scyliorhinid shark species commonly found in Mediterranean and Northeastern Atlantic waters. The philopatric and sedentary nature of female S. canicula, along with its high abundance among bottom trawl bycatch; stock exploitation resilience and widespread distribution could support the xenobiotic biomonitoring potential of this species. A year long study was performed from November 2019 to November 2020 within which 300 mature female specimens were gathered. Intramuscular Cu, Pb and Cd concentrations were determined via graphite furnace atomic absorption spectroscopy (GFAAS), while the digestive tract of each captured individual was pre-treated via alkaline extraction and vacuum filtration for its subsequent visual characterisation and polymer species Identification via RAMAN spectroscopy. Stable mean concentrations of Pb, Cd and Cu were observed in muscle tissues throughout the year with significant differences occurring only between non consecutive months. Spatial analysis shows the existence of well-defined heavy metal concentration hotspots occurring in certain points of the study site within which certain individuals surpassed the 0.05 and 0.3 µg·g-1 (ww) maximum threshold for safe human consumption stablished by the European commission Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006). Macroplastics, mesoplastic and microplastics were identified within Scyliorhinus canicula gastric tracts with plastic counts ranging between 3 to 32 units. Different plastic polymers were identified, with a higher presence of Polyethylene terephthalate (PET), Polyamide (PA) and polypropylene (PP).

abstract_text: Global climate change has fundamental impacts on the structure and function of marine environments. Examining the associated effects on threatened species using these environments is a major challenge for scientists and conservationists. This study investigated the effects of the 2016 extreme temperature event on the apparent survival and body condition of juvenile populations of two threatened carcharhinid shark species using a nursery habitat at St Joseph atoll, Seychelles. 228 blacktip reef sharks Carcharhinus melanopterus and 189 sicklefin lemon sharks Negaprion acutidens were caught during mark-recapture experiments over four years from 2014-2017. Mark-recapture modelling was used to estimate apparent survival (φ) and probability of recapture (p) for both species. Best-fit models indicated distinct differences around the 2016 thermal event with a 12% reduction in apparent survival of C. melanopterus (φ - 2014 + 15 = 0.65, φ - 2016+2017 = 0.53) and a 14% reduction in N. acutidens (φ – 2014, 15, 17 = 0.82, φ - 2016 = 0.68). Fulton’s condition factor was used estimate changes in body condition over the study period and evidenced significant decreases in body condition around the thermal event for both species. Findings from this study indicate a significant effect of large-scale ocean warming events on the fitness and survival of juvenile shark populations. How to tackle this ubiquitous threat will be a key question for shark science moving forward.

title: Assessing the global geographical overlap between filter-feeding megafaunal elasmobranchs and plastic pollution
abstract_text:
Plastic is ubiquitous in the environment and is known to have negative impacts on marine ecosystems. Marine organisms can entangle in discarded fishing gear, ingest plastic debris, and accumulate leached toxic chemicals in their tissues. Filter-feeding megafaunal elasmobranchs, including the reef manta ray (Mobula alfredi), giant manta ray (Mobula birostris), whale shark (Rhincodon typus) and basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) are exposed to the risk of plastic pollution, due to their low trophic level and their habitat overlap with known areas of plastic accumulation. They are also important flagship species for conservation with an additional value for ecotourism.

This piece of work explores the global geographical overlap between these species and plastic distribution to identify the populations at risk. We use publicly available databases of species occurrences to build a maximum entropy distribution model for the four species. We then overlay those with plastic debris data, including macroplastics such as discarded fishing gear, and microplastics distributions from existing plastic dispersal model outputs. This allows us to calculate the exposure of the four species to the risks of plastic ingestion and entanglement in discarded fishing gear.

This overlap analysis will allow us to build testable predictions of ingestion and entanglement risk based on overlap between debris and filter-feeder distributions, and in the future assess these predictions by evaluating existing evidence of exposure at different locations. We also hope the results of this study will focus mitigation policies and actions to the relevant priority locations.

title: Fish and ships: Soundscaping urban shark nurseries
abstract_text: Sound in the marine environment is used across taxa to inform behaviour, however human activities now often pollute natural cuescapes, masking or modifying important information. Anthropogenic disruption of marine sensory landscapes is known to negatively affect the distribution, behaviour and physiology of marine mammals, teleost fish and various invertebrate phyla. While relatively little is known about the mechanisms and capabilities of hearing in sharks, multiple studies have shown that they detect and respond (physiologically and behaviourally) to low frequency sounds (<1500 Hz). During juvenile development, sharks often display site fidelity to coastal habitats, such as mangroves, coral reefs and seagrass beds, where human disturbance can often be concentrated. One extreme example of this is in the Biscayne Bay, Miami, USA, where there is a high density and diversity of sharks along a heavily developed coastline with high levels of boating activity. Understanding which sounds sharks detect, respond to and are influenced by in situ has received little attention. To address this knowledge gap, we present the characterisation of the Biscayne Bay soundscape from an elasmobranch perspective (i.e. mapping spatial and temporal patterns of acoustic conditions at low frequencies, including in the particle motion domain). Specific attention is paid to describing the biological and anthropogenic contributions to the soundscape that fall within known hearing sensitivities. Our results are discussed in the context of potential ecological roles of sound in shark ecology and the impacts of anthropogenic noise on sharks. We will use this opportunity to open conversations on how deepening our understanding of elasmobranch sensory systems and multi-sensory integration may be applied to conservation initiatives.

title: Plastic ingestion in two syntopic species of deep-sea sharks from central Mediterranean
abstract_text: Plastics are synthetic materials made by long-life polymers, that persist for hundreds of years in the environment. This is the real plastic pollution problem. Every year enormous amounts of plastic debris are poured in the marine environment. In this work we investigated the presence of plastic remains in the stomach contents of three populations of Scyliorhinus canicula and Galeus melastomus, two of the most common deep demersal shark species in Mediterranean, along the Tyrrhenian coast of Italy. Both shark species have an opportunistic benthic scavenger behaviour. We obtained animals thanks to MEDITS survey and stomach contents were analysed in laboratory under a microscope. We discriminated plastic by shape (fibres, scrapes, sphere, and film) and colour (orange, black, white, blue, yellow, red, grey and green). The most common plastic remains founded in stomach were scrapes in both sharks’ populations in Lazio, film for lesser spotted dogfish and fibres for blackmouth catshark in Tuscany, and fibers for Scyliorhinus canicula and films for Galeus melastomus in Liguria. About colour discrimination, Scyliorhinus canicula ingested more grey and yellow plastics in the three populations than Galeus melastomus, which ingested, on the contrary, more black and white fragments. Ingestion seemed to be accidental for shapes, but for colours maybe the feeding behaviour of the two species could affect the choice.

title: Shark occurrence around Australia: now and into the future

authors.affiliation: Australian Institute of Marine Science and James Cook University

abstract_text: Many of the world’s shark populations are in decline indicating the need for improved conservation and management. A better understanding of their distribution and habitat requirements is vital for habitat protection and effective fisheries management, essential to maintain viable populations. Alongside this, oceans are warming worldwide and how such temperature variation will influence sharks requires investigation. We used statistical modelling tools to assess occurrence, habitat suitability and potential climate change effects for pelagic sharks from the Carcharhinidae and Lamnidae families in Australian waters and the adjacent high seas using shark occurrence records compiled from offshore commercial fisheries. We collated environmental and spatial predictors known to affect shark occurrence and developed generalised linear models to determine the extent of suitable habitat for pelagic sharks within the Australian continental Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). As well managed and appropriately located marine protected areas (MPAs) may enhance shark conservation, we quantified the amount of suitable habitat contained within existing MPAs. Our results indicate sea surface temperature (SST) to be a significant predictor of pelagic shark distribution, and even though highly suitable habitat was limited in MPA zones closed to fishing, Australia has strict fisheries legislation protecting pelagic sharks. With SST an important determinant of pelagic shark habitat suitability, we then examined the impact of increasing ocean temperatures in the future using an ensemble of climate models under two emission scenarios. Our predictions highlight how future SSTs are likely to shift the location of suitable pelagic shark habitat for both shark families within the Australian EEZ.

title: Assessment of metal pollution in batoids near a western Mediterranean coastal lagoon
abstract_text: Concerning pollution, non-essential metals have been historically present in the Mediterranean, sometimes reaching levels that could be harmful for marine biota. Despite the fact that batoids are a significant part of Mediterranean food webs, little is known about the threats that this metal pollution may represent to this group. In this study, we analyzed mercury (Hg), lead (Pb) and cadmium (Cd), in livers and muscle from 90 batoids of three different species: Dasyatis pastinaca (N=30), Myliobatis aquila (N=30) and, Torpedo torpedo (N=30). Our aim was to quantify these metals in a historically polluted area, the coast next to l’Albufera (East Spain), a coastal lagoon that discharges water into the sea. Besides, we studied whether metal concentration could be correlated with the different position in the food web of these species and with their size. In general, mercury was the most abundant metal, closely followed by lead and, lastly, cadmium was found in very low concentrations (mean±SD w.w. in muscle: 31.4±11.2 µg/g of Hg; 16.51±4.8 µg/g of Pb and 0.33±0.2 µg/g of Cd; in liver: 31.4±11.2 µg/g of Hg; 16.51±4.8 µg/g of Pb and 0.33±0.2 µg/g of Cd). Regarding biometric parameters, D. pastinaca and T. torpedo showed the highest metal concentration; in accordance to their higher position in the foodweb, in comparison with M. aquila. Results indicate that these batoids do not seem to be threatened by metals in the area, possibly reflecting either a low metallic pollution of their surroundings or their low mobilization from the sediments.

title: Moving North, season 1 - Are deep-sea sharks affected by warming water?
abstract_text: Continental shelf and deep ocean waters are subjected to anthropogenic pressures such as fishing and climate change-related environmental stressors. Sharks s in temperate waters are predicted to move poleward in response to climate change. However, their distribution through space and time remains poorly understood, limiting the potential to understand how they are responding to environmental stressors. Knowledge of the abundance and its environmental drivers of this threatened marine group is needed to inform sustainable management. Generalized additive models and mapping were performed on a 26-year scientific survey time-series in the Norwegian Sea and environmental data to model the impact of climate change on the distribution and abundance of two shark species living in deep and cold waters: Etmopterus spinax, and Galeus melastomus, at the northern fringe of their ranges, together with the distribution of their potential prey species. Both shark species significantly shifted their abundance northwards, and local abundances have declined to various degrees over the last seven years. The warming of northern waters across the last three decades seems the main driver of a northward shift in the local abundance of these two shark species and their prey. This indicates that climate change is likely a major driver of large-scale abundance patterns for sharks, even among deep-sea species. In a global warming context, survey data, long-term series and international cooperation are required to record extended shifts and better conserve transboundary species.

abstract_text: The Bull Shark, Carcharhinus leucas, faces varying levels of exploitation in fisheries and shark control programs around the world. Baseline information regarding the species’ life-history, reproductive behaviour and global or regional connectivity is crucial to evaluate fishery impacts and its conservation status. In this study, we obtained samples from nearly 1,000 sharks from 19 different sampling locations for the first global-scale assessment of population structure in this cosmopolitan species. Using a recently developed DNA capture approach (DArTcap), all samples were genotyped for 3,400 nuclear markers. In addition, the full mitochondrial genomes of 384 Indo-Pacific samples were also sequenced. Reproductive isolation was inferred at an ocean basin scale (eastern Pacific, western Atlantic, eastern Atlantic, Indo-West Pacific) with signals of separate island populations (Japan and Fiji). Bull Sharks appear to maintain reproductive connectivity using shallow coastal waters as dispersal corridors, whereas large oceanic distances and historical land bridges act as barriers. The removal of Bull Sharks from insular populations, such as Japan and Fiji, may precipitate local decline that cannot readily be replenished by immigration, which can in turn affect ecosystem dynamics. We note that females tend to return to the same area for reproduction, which makes them more vulnerable to local threats and an important focus for management actions. Finally, we provide new genetic markers that can assign provenance and sex from DNA samples which will prove valuable for future monitoring of the international fin and meat trade.

abstract_text: Oceanic (Mobula birostris) and reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) are among the most iconic species in our oceans yet significant knowledge gaps remain about fundamental aspects of their biology. For example, it remains a mystery both how their widespread distributions have arisen and the extent to which populations are connected within them. This information is crucial not only for establishing appropriate spatial scales for management, but for assessing population viability into the future. We address this using high-resolution genomic data for over 200 manta ray samples (M. birostris: n = 120, M. alfredi: n = 126) collected from across their entire distribution. We show that despite their recent divergence, oceanic and reef mantas display striking differences in population structure at a global scale, which is associated with significantly different levels of genetic diversity both between and within species. These findings indicate fundamental differences in colonisation strategy and migratory behaviour and highlight potentially vulnerable populations in need of heightened protection. We will examine these results in light of what is currently known about manta rays and discuss our findings in the context of global conservation management.
