abstract_text: Blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus) are a widespread Indo-Pacific reef shark species listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List for endangered species because of poaching, habitat loss and anthropogenic perturbations. Around the Island of Moorea (French Polynesia), the Center for Island Research and Environmental Observatory (CRIOBE) sampled 1700 adult and juvenile blacktip reef shark fin clips over a 13-year timespan. In Moorea, blacktip reef sharks give birth in shallow coastal lagoon areas, enabling neonate and juvenile sharks to withstand predation and to find sufficient foraging resources. For this PhD project, parentage analysis was conducted on the 1700 fin clip samples using genetic analyses (microsatellite DNA markers) to reconstruct the pedigree of the population. The resulting genealogy aims at defining life history traits such as the number of juveniles per litter, mother offspring resource allocation at birth (by using body condition and blood metabolite data), longevity and juvenile survival rates. The pedigree will also enable to evaluate the recruitment success of adult individuals (when offspring of an adult individual reaches adulthood), natal philopatry (females returning to their birthplace to parturition) in adult female individuals and the presence of dominant individuals (individuals which, on average, have higher reproduction rates) within the population. The results will provide a better understanding of the functioning of blacktip reef shark populations making it possible to provide information to local decision makers on the best strategies that can be developed to improve reef shark conservation.

title: Non-capture methods reveal blue shark population genetics in the UK

authors.affiliation: Celtic Deep, Marine Conservation & Research Foundation, Newcastle University

abstract_text: Despite blue sharks (Prionace glauca) being the most prevalent and most fished of any shark species, our understanding of their population genetic structure is limited. Large-scale genetic sampling is an important tool for the conservation and management of vulnerable and elusive species and can provide greater insight into estimates of population structure, abundance, and even behavioural ecology. While traditional genetics studies have relied more heavily on invasive techniques and expertise, novel non-invasive genetic sampling can offer an effective substitute. Furthermore, less invasive techniques have the potential to increase genetic studies’ applications whilst reducing costs. This study determined the efficacy and application of using a novel non-invasive technique to collect genetic material from free-swimming blue sharks for population genetic studies. The study took place in the Celtic Sea, UK, where we collected 39 epidermal swabs from a total of 11 free-swimming blue sharks using a toothbrush and freediving approach. Regions of the mitochondrial CO1 and control region, and nuclear ribosomal ITS2 regions, were successfully amplified from the samples. Results across all three markers support the existence of low genetic variation between regions, however, genetic structuring remains a possibility that requires further investigation. Results from the mitochondrial control region showed the correct identification of individuals across multiple samples, demonstrating this method’s application for long-term mark-recapture studies. We recommend future studies investigate contamination mitigation, improvement of amplification techniques, and determine the application of samples for other population genomics analyses, such as high throughput sequencing.

title: Genetic diversity and population structure of Raja clavata in the North-East Atlantic
abstract_text: Thornback Ray (Raja clavata) is a relatively abundant commercial skate species occurring in coastal waters of the North-East Atlantic and Mediterranean, listed by the IUCN as Near Threatened. It is the dominant skate species caught in commercial fisheries in northern European seas. Historically, regional population declines have been observed, although increased landings indicate increases in population size in several areas over recent decades. This study describes the genetic diversity and population structure of Raja clavata hierarchically among ecoregions, spanning the Greater North Sea (GNS), Celtic Sea (CS), and Bay of Biscay and Iberian coast (BB), as well as within ecoregions by ICES Divisions. Over 8000 samples were collected (2004 – 2022) and genotyped. Subsequent quality control resulted in a SNP dataset of >4000 SNPs for analyses. Estimates of genetic diversity are provided among and within ecoregions. Small yet significant genetic differentiation was evident globally (Fst,global = 0.0042) and among all ecoregions via pairwise Fst (Fst,GNS-CS = 0.003, Fst,CS-BB = 0.007, Fst,GNS-BB = 0.009; p-values < 0.01). Only ICES Divisions 4b and 4c in the GNS (Fst,4b-4c = 0.00004, p = 0.144) showed no significant genetic differentiation within ecoregions. AMOVA, discriminant component analysis, and admixture modelling provide further evidence and describe the population structure on both hierarchical population levels investigated. This is the largest known genetic study of Raja clavata, to our knowledge. This research helps to inform stock identification and thus assessment, conservation and fisheries management, by accounting for genetic population structure at different spatial scales in the North-East Atlantic.

abstract_text: Influence of environmental factors on prey discrimination of bait-attracted white sharks were studied over a six-year period (2008-2013) at Dyer Island Nature Reserve (Gansbaai, South Africa). This work deepens previous published study on surface predatory behaviour of bait-attracted white sharks conducted in the same area where, from 240 predator-prey interactions observed in the same period, both immature and mature white sharks were attracted from the seal shaped decoy rather than the tuna bait, except for the years 2008 and 2011. Tide ranges, underwater visibility, water temperature, and sea conditions are, in decreasing order, the factors that drive white sharks to the prey choice. High tide reduces the minimum depth from which sharks could approach seals close to the shore, while a good visibility helps the sharks to use their vision ability to implement predatory choices to energetical richer prey, the odorless seal shaped decoy. On the contrary, warmer water is associated both with an increasing and diversity of teleosts which are prey of white sharks and to an increase of phytoplankton that reduces the underwater visibility, driving them to the tuna bait choice. Finally, sea condition was almost always slightly rough, ensuring a good average underwater visibility. Recommendations for future research work at this site are presented.

abstract_text: Many elasmobranchs exhibit complex courtship rituals. The function of large aggregations of basking sharks engaged in circling behaviour largely remains a mystery. We present, underwater and aerial video recordings of multiple circling groups of basking sharks in late summer (August to September) during years 2016–2021 in Ireland. Groups comprised females and males numbering between 6 and 23 individuals that were not filter feeding. Grouped sharks swam slowly in a clockwise or anticlockwise rotating ‘torus’ (diameter range: 17–39 m) consisting of circling individuals layered vertically from the surface to a maximum depth of 16 m. Within a torus, sharks engaged in close-following, echelon, close flank-approach or parallel swimming behaviours. Total body lengths of circling sharks overlapped known lengths of sexually mature individuals. In some toruses female body coloration was paler than that of males. Within a torus individuals associated with most other members rapidly (within minutes) indicating toroidal behaviours facilitate multiple interactions. Torus members also interacted through fin-fin and fin-body contacts, rolling to expose ventral surfaces to following sharks, and breaching behaviour. We also confirmed that a torus forms from shark following behaviour, and can change rotation direction frequently. Collectively, our observations explain a courtship function for non-feeding circling groups. This study highlights the importance of coastal waters off western Ireland as critical habitats supporting courtship reproductive behaviour of endangered basking sharks, the first such habitats identified for this species globally. This has important conservation implications for a species recently given legal protection status in Ireland.

abstract_text: White shark movements are typically observed over large spatial scales (100s-1000s km2). However, observation of fine-scale movement behaviour of white sharks is necessary to improve our understanding of their usage of near-shore coastal areas where there is an increased probability of interactions between sharks and humans. Based on passive acoustic data from a dense, but non-triangulating, array we investigated the fine scale movement of white sharks at a coastal beach within a nursery area off Hawk’s Nest, New South Wales from 2010-2015. Using a spatial Hidden Markov Model (HMM) we were able to estimate white shark movement tracks during each shark visit to the array based on detection binning over 5-minute time intervals. The HMM also enabled direct estimation of the probability of detection as a function of distance from shark to acoustic receivers. The HMM-estimated movement tracks predict heavy utilisation of very shallow water close to the high-water mark by the sharks. Additionally, the southern end of the beach appears to be a focus for short term white shark residency at the beach. The movement tracks estimated here allowed the first high-resolution investigation of white shark movements in the Hawk’s Nest nursery area and demonstrate the potential for estimation of fine-scale position data from non-triangulating passive acoustic monitoring arrays deployed in other coastal marine areas.

title: Making a Difference: how to realize policy change

authors.affiliation: Irish Basking Shark Group; George Mason University

abstract_text:
Shark research and conservation efforts are typically driven by a desire to inform the status assessment and increase the level of protection afforded to the target species. However, the translation of scientific findings and or conservation initiatives into real world policy change is a persistent challenge for non-governmental organisations and academics. Basking sharks are listed by the IUCN as globally endangered. Ireland is significant to basking sharks in the Northeast Atlantic, however until 2022, they were not protected under domestic legislation. To help others overcome this disconnect we describe and review the methods that the Irish Basking Shark Group (IBSG), a volunteer research and outreach organisation, deployed to realize a change in legislative status for the species in Irish waters.

Between 2009 and 2022 the IBSG delivered approximately forty research, outreach and legislative change initiatives designed to raise the awareness, understanding and appreciation of basking sharks in Irish and International waters. No individual action or effort stream (i.e., public outreach, scientific research or political lobbying) delivered alone. Rather an integrated approach that melded internationally significant research studies with locally orientated ocean literacy initiates’ and strategically timed media campaigns provided the maximum leverage of policy makers.

Lastly, we consider how these experiences can be applied to other species or scaled up to regional forums. Our goal here is to provide a road map for similar conservation efforts through sharing our experience in attaining protection for the basking shark in Irish wildlife legislation, the first fish to be given this status.

title: Capture heats up sharks
abstract_text: Catch-and-release fishing is an important component of ecotourism industries and scientific research worldwide, but its total impact on animal physiology, health and survival is understudied for many species of sharks. We combined biologging and blood chemistry to explore how this fisheries interaction influenced the physiology of two widely distributed, highly migratory shark species: blue sharks (Prionace glauca), and tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier). Nineteen sharks were caught by drum line or rod-and-reel angling; subcutaneous body temperature measurements were taken immediately upon capture, with 6 individuals also providing subsequent subcutaneous body temperature measurements via biologging as they swam freely for several hours post-release. We found that short-term capture caused shark body temperature to increase significantly and rapidly, with increases of 0.6 – 2.7°C for blue sharks (mean 1.2 ± 0.6°C) and 0.5 – 0.9°C for tiger sharks (mean 0.7 ± 0.2°C), and with capture-induced heating rates of blue sharks averaging 0.3°C min-1 but as high as 0.8°C min-1. These heating rates were 3-8 times faster than maximum rates encountered by our biologging sharks swimming through thermally stratified waters. Biologging data showed that body temperatures underwent gradual decline after release, returning to match water temperatures approximately 10 – 40 mins post-release. Blood biochemistry showed variable lactate/glucose levels following capture; however, these concentrations weren’t correlated with the magnitude of body temperature increase, nor body size or hooking time. These perturbations of the natural state could have immediate and longer-term effects on the welfare and ecology of sharks caught and future research could focus on exploring these effects.
